analysis.one_liner: Caps interest and fees on consumer loans at 36% a year nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap consumer loan rates at 36% was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in July 2008, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written a single national limit of 36% into federal law for nearly all consumer lending, counting every fee, add-on product, and insurance charge as part of the rate. Loans made above that cap would have been uncollectible in court, with criminal penalties for lenders and enforcement power for state attorneys general. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never moved again before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who currently pay triple-digit rates: people using payday loans, car-title loans, refund-anticipation loans, and high-rate credit cards. Anyone charged fees that push the true cost of borrowing past 36% would keep that money, and loans above the cap could not be enforced against them.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any creditor from extending consumer credit at an annual rate above 36%, and counts fees, late fees, over-limit fees, cash advance fees, membership fees, credit insurance premiums, and ancillary product charges toward that rate [S2] [S3].

Makes any payment on a loan made in violation of the cap null and void, requiring the lender to return principal, interest, and fees and void any security interest, and lets a borrower raise the violation as a defense at any time [S3].

Attaches criminal penalties of one year in prison and a fine of the greater of triple the accrued debt or $50,000 per violation, and lets state attorneys general sue to enforce the cap within three years [S2] [S3].
Leaves state consumer-protection laws in place, so states with tighter caps or stronger rules keep them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-cost lenders: payday and car-title loan chains, subprime credit card issuers, and any lender whose business model depends on rates and fees above 36%. Some marginal borrowers could also lose access to credit entirely if lenders stop serving high-risk customers rather than lend at the capped rate.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday lenders and high-rate credit issuers

drawbacks.text: Lenders facing a hard 36% cap could simply stop making small, short-term loans to risky borrowers, leaving some people with no credit option in an emergency [S3].

A single national ceiling would apply to all states regardless of local cost conditions, and criminal exposure for every above-cap transaction (up to a $50,000 fine or triple the debt per violation) is a stiff enforcement design that industry would argue chills legitimate high-risk lending [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is large and direct: every dollar of interest and fees above 36% stops being collectible, which targets exactly the products that trap borrowers in repeat cycles. The main honest trade-off is access — some borrowers who today pay very high rates might find no lender willing to serve them at the cap. Whether that gap is better filled by public alternatives was not addressed in the bill. On balance the protection outweighs the access loss, but the bill never got a hearing, so the design was never tested or refined.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee in July 2008, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill on July 17, 2008, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S1] [S5].
No further action was ever taken on the bill — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — and it expired with the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009 [S5] [S1].
It carried only one cosponsor in the Senate [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday, car-title, and high-rate credit card lenders are better off: with no national cap enacted, they kept the legal ability to charge rates and fees above 36% and to enforce those loans in court. Borrowers paying those rates gained nothing because the bill never advanced past referral.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-cost lenders kept charging above-cap rates

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 17, 2008 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Senate cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it drew no other Senate support on the record.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Christopher Dodd (D-CT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: Payday lending and high-rate credit card industries
against.role: Lenders whose rates would exceed the 36% cap
against.what_they_did: Opposed national usury caps; the bill drew no Republican or additional Democratic cosponsors during its five-and-a-half-month life.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a recorded vote. Both its sponsor and its single cosponsor were Democrats, and it drew no other support from either party while pending.

industries.industry: Payday, car-title, and other high-cost small-dollar lenders
industries.note: A 36% all-in cap, with voided loans and criminal penalties, would make their core product unenforceable and unprofitable. These lenders profit by charging rates and fees that routinely exceed the cap, and every dollar they keep is a dollar a struggling borrower pays.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer finance companies
industries.note: Late fees, over-limit fees, cash advance fees, annual fees, and credit insurance premiums would all count toward the 36% rate, shrinking penalty-fee income and forcing lower headline rates on subprime lending. Card fee income is borne directly by cardholders, most heavily those who carry balances or miss payments.
The bill gave state attorneys general a new three-year federal enforcement tool against usurious loans, while preserving stronger state consumer protections.
